title: Basie as father figure: 'pregnant nineteenths'
summary: Basie called him Junior, and taught by example, telling him to keep arrangements simple.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Just one other thing, how much of a personal loss was it for you?

It was as though I had lost a relative, because I felt like he was a father in a sense. He used to call me “Junior” all the time. So he gave me a feeling of being one of his sons. He called Joe Williams -- he would refer to Joe Williams as his number one son. I almost thought of myself as being his number two son, because of all the things that he was able to teach me without actually teaching, but just through example and telling me, “Keep the pregnant nineteenths out of there and make it simple.” That was how Basie schooled me.
Run that past me again now. Keep the who, what -­
In the writing arrangements he would say, “We don’t want too many of those pregnant nineteenths in there,” and what he meant was that the thing is too busy, just being too busy.
Right. You got too much shit in this chord.

Yeah, too much going on. That’s how he put it. “Pregnant nineteenths and keep it simple. Give me a simple life. It’s the little things that mean so much.” Those were -- that’s the way he would -- that was his textbook.
So in other words, his instructions were succinct, but yet as pithy or substantive as his -- the little stuff he dropped.
